## Introduction

In this activity, you complete and render a short report
that reads the summary written by your pipeline. The report is
partially completed: its methods are written, and you add the
confidence interval, an interpretation, and the provenance fields. By
the end, you should be able to explain where each number in the
report came from and what a reader needs to recreate it.

You need the `meta-summary.csv` file from the
[targets activity](05_targets.qmd#targets-checkpoint).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Get back on track {#recover-report}

If you arrived late, lost your session, or broke a working file, run this
from the project root in the **R Console**. It selects the full dataset,
backs up your working pipeline in `workspace/`, and rebuilds the summary
with the reference pipeline. Any report edits you have already made are kept.

``` r
source("pipelines/recover_workshop.R")
```
:::

After recovery, start the report exercise at Step 1. If Quarto reports an
error, look for the first error and the reported line or chunk in `report.qmd`.

## Step 1: copy and render the template

Copy and render your report using the code below. Run the same render command after each
edit. If you want to restart from the template, rename your existing
`workspace/report.qmd` in the **Files** pane before running this block.

```{r health-quarto-render-template, eval = FALSE}
source("pipelines/workshop_support.R")
use_workshop_book_outputs()

dir.create("workspace", showWarnings = FALSE)
report <- file.path("workspace", "report.qmd")
if (!file.exists(report)) {
  stopifnot(file.copy("pipelines/exercise/health_wellbeing_report.qmd", report))
}
render_workshop_report()
```

Next, open the `report.html`. If you started from the template,
the pooled estimate appears along with three **TODO** markers.

```{r health-quarto-view-rendered-template-view-html, eval = FALSE}
browseURL(
  file.path("workspace", "report.html")
)
```

## Step 2: read the report source

Allow up to 10 minutes for this activity.

Open `workspace/report.qmd` in RStudio.

```{r health-quarto-view-rendered-template-edit, eval = FALSE}
file.edit(
  file.path("workspace", "report.qmd")
)
```

The pipeline performs the analysis, while the report explains its methods and
interprets the saved result. Because the report never retypes a
number, rerunning the pipeline and rendering again updates every
value.

## Step 3: complete the three gaps

The Results section reports two 95%
intervals that answer different questions:

-   The **confidence interval** describes uncertainty in the
    *average* association across studies. It usually narrows as
    studies are added.
-   The **prediction interval** describes where the true association
    in a new, comparable study is likely to fall under the model. It
    adds the between-study variance, $\tau^2$, so it stays wide when the
    studies differ.

I² is the percentage of variation in the study estimates that is due
to between-study heterogeneity rather than sampling error.
Use these definitions to write TODO 2 in your own words.

Edit `workspace/report.qmd` and save it.

-   **TODO 1**, in Results: report the confidence interval using inline
    R code, following the pattern for the pooled correlation.
-   **TODO 2**, in Results: explain how the prediction interval and
    confidence interval answer different questions.
-   **TODO 3**, in Provenance: add list items for the dataset pin
    version and the pipeline script MD5.

Render the report again after updating the `report.qmd` file:

```{r health-quarto-render-iterative, eval = FALSE}
render_workshop_report()
browseURL(
  file.path("workspace", "report.html")
)
```

Solutions are below:

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

## Solution to TODO 1

Replace the sentence about the pooled correlation and the TODO 1
paragraph with:

```  markdown
The pooled correlation was `r knitr::inline_expr('sprintf("%.3f", result$pooled_r)')` with a
`r knitr::inline_expr('sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * result$confidence_level)')` confidence interval
from `r knitr::inline_expr('sprintf("%.3f", result$ci_lower)')` to
`r knitr::inline_expr('sprintf("%.3f", result$ci_upper)')`.
``` 
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Example for TODO 2

Your wording can differ. For example:

```  markdown
The confidence interval describes uncertainty in the average association.
The prediction interval describes plausible true associations in a
comparable setting under the model.
``` 
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution to TODO 3

```  markdown
-   Dataset pin version: `r knitr::inline_expr('result$data_version')`
-   Pipeline script MD5: `r knitr::inline_expr('pipeline_md5')`
``` 
:::

The completed reference report is
`pipelines/health_wellbeing_report.qmd`. If you are stuck, compare
your copy with it.

```{r health-quarto-view-rendered-template-edit-complete, eval = FALSE}
file.edit(
  file.path("pipelines", "health_wellbeing_report.qmd")
)
```

## Step 4: render again and check the numbers

Reload `report.html` in your browser. Then compare its values with the
summary file:

```{r health-quarto-summary, include = TRUE, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, cache = FALSE, output = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
summary_csv <- read.csv(
  file.path(workshop_output_dir(), "meta-summary.csv")
)
summary_csv[, c("data_version", "studies", "pooled_r", "ci_lower", "ci_upper")]
```

Run this code to render the report and open it in your browser.

```{r health-quarto-render-final, eval = FALSE}
render_workshop_report()
browseURL(
  file.path("workspace", "report.html")
)
```

An approved HTML report can be served from a project site or attached
to a release. Before sharing, review the report for any content that
came from data with reuse conditions. The report source, versioned
analysis code, metadata, and environment record help others
understand how the published HTML was made.

## Publishing and journal formats {#quarto-publishing}

Quarto extensions add formats and templates for particular publishing
workflows. Browse the
[Journal Articles extension listing](https://quarto.org/docs/extensions/listing-journals.html)
and find a format relevant to your field. Examples include:

| Extension | Article style or publisher |
| --- | --- |
| `apaquarto` | American Psychological Association, seventh edition |
| `elsevier` | Elsevier journals |
| `plos` | Public Library of Science |
| `jss` | Journal of Statistical Software |

Open an extension's repository to check its supported formats,
required software, author metadata, and usage instructions. Compare
the template with the target journal's current submission guidance.

To try one, create a separate article directory and start from the
[Elsevier template](https://github.com/quarto-journals/elsevier): 

```{bash add-quarto-template, eval = FALSE, output = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
rm -rf health-wellbeing-article
mkdir -p health-wellbeing-article
cd health-wellbeing-article
quarto use template quarto-journals/elsevier --no-prompt
```

The template supplies an example QMD, bibliography, and extension
files. Elsevier supports `elsevier-html` and `elsevier-pdf`; the PDF format also
requires a LaTeX installation. 

Open the downloaded Elsevier template file:

```{r health-quarto-view-rendered-template, eval = FALSE}
elsevier_path <- file.path("health-wellbeing-article", "health-wellbeing-article.qmd")
file.edit(
  elsevier_path
)
```

And we can render this document as a PDF.

```{r render-quarto-template, eval = FALSE, output = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
system2("quarto", c("render", shQuote(elsevier_path), "--to", "elsevier-pdf"))

browseURL(
  file.path("health-wellbeing-article", "health-wellbeing-article.pdf")
)
```

Extensions are stored locally in `_extensions/`. Include that folder
with the article source in Git. For a release, record the Quarto and
extension versions alongside the R package versions in `renv.lock`.
See the Quarto guidance on installing and versioning extensions
[@quarto-managing-extensions].
